Nematodes can increase soil fertility, primarily through their role in nutrient cycling — breaking down organic matter and releasing essential nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus that plants can absorb [d3][d5]. Some nematode species are particularly well-known for enhancing soil health by protecting plant roots from pathogens and improving the structure of the soil matrix [d4][d1]. Yes, iodine supplementation can cause thyroid problems, as it may precipitate hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, goiter, and/or thyroid autoimmunity in some individuals, particularly those with preexisting thyroid disease or a history of iodine deficiency [d3][d5]. Research has shown that iodine supplementation during pregnancy could raise cord blood TSH levels by 27.3% and was associated with a 2.5-fold increased risk of TSH above 3 mIU/L in mothers consuming 200 µg or more daily [d2], and Merck Manuals notes that excess iodine can sometimes cause the thyroid gland to become overactive (hyperthyroidism) or underactive (hypothyroidism), though the risk is generally higher in those previously deficient [d4]. However, a non-iodine-deficient population can tolerate excess iodine quite well, and the majority of cases do not result in clinically fatal consequences — though susceptibility can be increased in specific groups such as those with autoimmune thyroid disease, the elderly, and fetuses [d1][d3].
[[END-OF-ANSWER]]
